guides.title: Gym diary POV: a vertical vlog shot at arm's length
guides.desc: A redhead in a grey crop top talks to her own camera between sets — a floor stretch, a deep side lunge, a look at the protein shaker, an overhead stretch, then the gym bag slung over her shoulder on the way out. Vertical, handheld, no tripod anywhere in the frame.

steps.title: Put the camera in her hand, not on a tripod
steps.text: A tripod shot of a gym is stock footage. An arm's-length shot of the same gym is a diary. Say where the camera is — held in her own hand, close, wide, slightly tilted — and accept that her shoulder and forearm will crop the frame. That crop is the format.
steps.prompt: Vertical 9:16 handheld phone video, first-person vlog. A young woman with red hair in a ponytail, grey sports bra and cream long-sleeve crop, dark leggings, sits on the floor of a dim gym. She holds the phone herself at arm's length: wide lens, close to her face, slight tilt, her forearm and shoulder entering the bottom of the frame. Background: racks of dumbbells, dark ceiling, scattered downlights. Natural handheld shake, no stabilisation, no camera moves that a hand cannot make.
steps.result_caption: Her forearm crops the bottom of the frame and the lens is a hand's length from her face — that is the whole format, before a single beat happens.

steps.title: Give her a routine, not a workout
steps.text: Nobody films their whole session. List the small beats instead — sit down, stretch, a side lunge, checking the shaker, shouldering the bag — and let them run out of order. Mundane beats are what a real diary is made of; a set-by-set workout reads as an ad.
steps.prompt: Beats, same woman and same gym throughout: (1) sits cross-legged on the floor, talks to the camera between sets. (2) Deep side lunge on the floor, holding the phone up with one hand. (3) Holds a clear shaker of milky-beige protein up near her face and looks at it, not at the lens. (4) Steps back from the phone and stretches both arms overhead — the only shot where her whole body is in frame. (5) Slings a black gym bag over her shoulder and looks into the lens on the way out. Keep her hair, top and leggings identical in every beat.
steps.result_caption: She looks at the shaker, stretches her arms overhead, leans back in to talk. Four seconds of nothing happening — that is the beat list working.

steps.title: Deliver vertical, not letterboxed
steps.text: Vertical source gets ruined by a 1080-tall pipeline: it comes out 607 px wide and soft. Cap the width instead — 720×1280 H.264 keeps the phone aspect, stays sharp on a phone and lands far under the size cap. Play the clip above.

guides.result: Fifteen vertical seconds that read as somebody's own phone footage: the arm is in shot, the framing is wrong on purpose, and nothing in it looks directed.

guides.title: Seoul street food through a fisheye: 15 seconds at the orange tent
guides.desc: A circular fisheye follows a girl down a Seoul side street into an orange pojangmacha tent — a steel tray of tteokbokki, a paper cup handed over the counter, then back out past the stalls as the light turns blue.

steps.title: Name the lens, not the mood
steps.text: "Nostalgic" and "retro" produce nothing. A circular fisheye with hard black corners produces an image you can recognise before you read the caption. Describe the optics — round image inside a black frame, extreme barrel distortion, close focus — and the era comes for free.
steps.prompt: Handheld camcorder footage through a circular fisheye lens: round image with hard black corners, extreme barrel distortion, straight lines bending, close focus, slight chromatic fringing, soft contrast. Subject: a young Korean woman in an olive jacket over a white hoodie, dark hair, walking a narrow Seoul side street in the early evening. Keep her jacket, hoodie and hair identical in every shot.
steps.result_caption: Round image, hard black corners — even a steel steam tray of tteokbokki bows at the edges. Crop this to 16:9 and it is ordinary food stock footage.

steps.title: One street, one stall, one cup
steps.text: Continuity is cheap when the location is small. Write the whole visit as a route through a single tent — the food before the face, the hand-off over the counter, eating standing up, then back out — and the model has nothing left to invent between shots. One paper cup carries the second half of the film; give it to her on camera and it can never appear out of nowhere.
steps.prompt: Route, same lens and same subject: (1) macro of tteokbokki — red-sauced rice cakes in a steel steam tray, the vendor out of focus behind it. (2) She takes a white paper cup of it from the vendor's hand across the steel counter, smiling. (3) Standing under the orange-and-blue striped tent, bare bulb overhead, eating from the cup with a wooden skewer. (4) Side view as she walks off, still eating from the same cup. (5) She walks down the middle of the street holding the cup up toward the lens, streetlights on, sky gone blue.
steps.result_caption: The cup is handed across the counter, then she is eating under the bulb. Showing the hand-off is why the cup can never appear out of nowhere later.

steps.title: Keep the 4:3 frame the lens was shot on
steps.text: The round image needs a near-square frame or the black corners get cropped into bars and the whole effect dies. Source is 1664×1248 — deliver it at 4:3, 1080 tall, and leave the vignette alone. Play the clip above.

guides.result: Fifteen seconds of believable found footage: round frame, black corners, one street, one stall, one cup — and a face that stays the same in every shot.

guides.title: Ankle-height fisheye: twelve shots of one all-white fit in 15 seconds
guides.desc: A circular fisheye sits on the pavement while a cream total-look walks over it — brick, roller shutters, graffiti. Between the walks: two beats from directly overhead, a macro of the white headphones, another of white wraparound shades, a wet night street, the block upside-down in a puddle, and a crew of three standing over the lens.

steps.title: Put the lens on the pavement, not at eye level
steps.text: A street fashion clip at eye level is a hundred other street fashion clips. Rest the circular fisheye on the ground and let the subject walk over it: white sneakers stay sharp in the middle of the round frame while the brick, the shutters and the graffiti bend away into the black corners. The camera position is the whole idea — nothing has to be styled to make the shot work.
steps.prompt: Circular fisheye lens: round image with hard black corners, extreme barrel distortion, straight lines bending hard. Camera resting on wet grey pavement, looking up and forward as a person walks over and past it — off-white baggy sweatpants, white sneakers, cream layers, black bucket hat, large white over-ear headphones. Narrow city street, red brick facade, metal roller shutters, graffiti on one wall, parked cars. Overcast daylight, handheld, no stabilisation.
steps.result_caption: The lens is on the ground: the sneaker is the nearest thing in frame, the brick and the roller shutters bend away into the black corners. Same street at eye level would be unremarkable.

steps.title: Twelve shots in fifteen seconds — write them as a flat list
steps.text: The longest shot here is under three seconds and most are barely one, so nothing has room to explain itself. Write the whole film as a numbered list where the outfit is the only constant, and keep coming back to the ankle-height camera between the detours. That return is what makes twelve unrelated framings read as one film instead of a mood-board.
steps.prompt: Shot list, same all-white fit and same circular fisheye throughout: (1)(2)(3) ground-level walks past red brick and graffitied roller shutters, white sneakers closest to the lens, parked cars behind. (4)(5) Straight down from above: the walker centred in the round frame, black bucket hat and white over-ear headphones, pavement filling the circle. (6) Extreme macro of the white headphone cup and headband, matte shell and brushed metal arm, black background. (7) Back to the pavement — a sneaker steps directly over the lens. (8) Extreme macro of white wraparound sport sunglasses on the face, the street reflected in the lenses. (9) Night: wet asphalt, car and street lights smeared in the reflections, cream trousers walking through. (10)(11) The block hanging upside-down in a puddle, ripples crossing the buildings. (12) Three people in white fits standing over the camera, arms out, brick wall behind them.
steps.result_caption: Four seconds, four shots — two from directly overhead, the headphone macro, then straight back down to pavement level. Nothing is held long enough to explain itself.

steps.title: Downscale once, at the very end
steps.text: The source is 3840×2160 at 70 Mbps — 133 MB for fifteen seconds. Grade at 4K, then take exactly one Lanczos pass down to 1080p H.264. A second resize somewhere in the middle of the chain is what turns the stretched fisheye edges into mush. Play the clip above.

guides.result: Fifteen seconds cut from twelve shots that keep returning to the same ankle-height camera, held together by one outfit and one lens.

guides.title: Polar Scalp: a 13-second shampoo ad with no model, no hands, no voiceover
guides.desc: Condensation on a cold bottle between ice cubes, a cucumber-and-mint water vortex, a silky cream wave, hair strands hit by a splash, the bottle in a water crown, then a flat navy end card. The whole spot is water and one bottle.

steps.title: Five macros beat one hero shot
steps.text: A single rotating bottle is a render, not an ad. Break the promise into separate physical close-ups — cold, fresh, rich, clean — and the product gets a new reason to be on screen each time. Water is the connective tissue: it moves in every shot, which is what lets hard cuts between unrelated macros read as one spot. Note that the bottle is absent from the middle of the film entirely; the cream wave and the hair splash carry it alone.
steps.prompt: Cosmetics commercial, macro, deep blue palette, studio light, dark background throughout. Shots: (1) a tall silver-white shampoo bottle covered in condensation, ice cubes and water droplets suspended around it, shallow depth of field, blue bokeh. (2) The same bottle standing inside a spinning vortex of clear water with cucumber slices and mint leaves orbiting it, backlit, a horizontal light streak behind it. (3) No product: a thick silky cream-white wave folding over itself on deep blue. (4) No product: extreme macro of straight dark hair strands as a sheet of water hits them, droplets in the air. (5) The bottle inside a rising crown of water, ice cube tumbling past the lens.
steps.result_caption: The middle of the ad, with no product in it at all: the tail of the vortex, a cream-white wave, then water hitting hair. Moving water is the only thing holding these cuts together.

steps.title: The label will lie — keep the small type out of focus
steps.text: Look at the frame below: the brand line survived, the sub-line under it came out as "ANTI ING ECALR". This happens on every label at every quality setting. The fix is compositional, not a better prompt — keep only the big brand word sharp, throw everything smaller into bokeh or shoot it edge-on, and replace real ingredient copy in post if it has to be legible.
steps.prompt: Label rule for every product shot: the brand word large, centred and sharp; all secondary copy small, low-contrast and outside the plane of focus. Never ask for a paragraph of ingredient text on the bottle.
steps.result_caption: Read the label: the brand line holds, the sub-line under it came out as "ANTI ING ECALR". Large type survives, small type does not.

steps.title: End on a flat card, not on the product
steps.text: The last frame is the only place typography is fully under your control — a plain navy card with the name and one line ("Feel the Ultimate Freshness") carries the branding the bottle could not. Deliver 1080p H.264. Play the clip above.

guides.result: A finished cosmetics spot built from five macro shots and one card — plus the honest version of what AI does to the small type on a label.

guides.title: Anatomy Atelier: a 3D organ explorer with a dissection slider
guides.desc: A dark reference app walked through heart, liver and eye — an organ rail on the left, a rotating specimen in the middle with clickable hotspots and an "Intact specimen" dissection slider under it, and a key-facts dossier on the right.

steps.title: Rail, stage, dossier — name the three columns first
steps.text: Most "explorer" briefs produce a gallery. Ask for three fixed columns instead and the app gets a spine: a scrollable rail of organs on the left, a single 3D stage in the middle, a facts panel on the right. One extra demand does the heavy lifting — every rail row carries the body system under the organ name, so the list teaches grouping before anything is clicked.
steps.prompt: Build a dark anatomy reference web app, "Anatomy Atelier". Three fixed columns. Left: a vertical rail of organ rows, each a small illustrated thumbnail, the organ name, and the body system in smaller grey type underneath — Heart / Cardiovascular, Brain / Nervous System, Lungs / Respiratory System, Liver / Digestive System, Kidneys / Urinary System, Eye / Sensory System, Intestine / Digestive System. The active row sits in a lifted rounded panel. Centre: a 3D stage with one photoreal organ specimen, slow auto-rotate, drag to orbit, near-black background. Right: a facts panel. Deep charcoal UI, coral accents.
steps.result_caption: Every rail row carries two lines — Liver, then Digestive System under it. The list groups the body before a single organ is opened.

steps.title: Fix the skeleton of the dossier, not the fields
steps.text: The usual advice is to keep identical fields for every item. That is wrong here: an eye has a diameter, a liver has a portal vein. Fix the *shape* instead — tagline, a KEY FACTS table, then two highlight cards — and let the keys inside change per organ. The user learns where to look once; the content stays medically honest.
steps.prompt: Right panel contract for every organ: organ name, a one-line epithet, a short paragraph on what it does, a KEY FACTS table of icon + key + value rows, then two highlight cards — "Medical importance" and "Did you know". The keys are chosen per organ, not shared: the eye reads Size, Weight, Daily, Location, Blood supply, Function. Selecting a different organ in the rail replaces the specimen and the panel contents; the panel order and position never change.
steps.result_caption: The eye's facts read Size, Weight, Daily, Location, Blood supply, Function. The liver's list is different — same panel, different keys.

steps.title: Make the slider the interaction, then record at 30 fps
steps.text: The control under the stage is a dissection depth slider that starts at "Intact specimen" — dragging it opens the specimen up, and hotspot dots on the model ("click a dot to explore") carry the rest. One continuous control beats a menu of layer checkboxes. Delivery: screen capture arrives at 60 fps, conform to 30 and the file halves with nothing visible lost. Play the clip above.

guides.result: A teaching app where the furniture never moves: switching organs swaps the specimen and the facts, and the dissection slider is the only thing that changes what you are looking at.

guides.title: Castlevania pixel-art series: 8 prompts, line by line
guides.desc: Eight 16-bit gothic scenes from one style block — castle gate, relic shrine, stat altar, equip altar, corridor fork, castle map, boss fight, throne room — each with the copy-paste prompt and the one sentence that made it work.

steps.title: 1. Castle gate — the opening shot
steps.text: This style block gets copied word-for-word into the seven prompts that follow. Everything after "Style:" is the series contract: chunky pixels, dithered shading, no anti-aliasing, cold moonlight against warm torchlight, and a flat ban on readable text.
steps.prompt:
A wide 16-bit pixel-art RPG scene in the style of classic Castlevania games. A lone vampire hunter in a tattered dark-blue coat, holding a long whip coiled at his belt, stands before towering wrought-iron gothic castle gates atop a cliff. A full blood-red moon glows behind jagged castle towers; bats circle overhead; thin fog rolls across cracked stone stairs leading up to the gate.
Style: classic 16-bit Castlevania pixel art, chunky readable pixels, moody gothic game-dev aesthetic, dithered shading, no anti-aliasing blur.
Lighting: cold blue moonlight contrasted with warm torchlight flanking the gate, deep purple-black night sky, dramatic rim light on the hunter's silhouette.
Composition: wide banner, hunter lower-left, castle gate dominating the right and center, strong vertical gothic architecture, cinematic RPG intro framing.
Constraints: no readable text anywhere, no logos, no watermark, no UI labels.

steps.title: 2. Relic shrine — four pillars
steps.text: How to render a list without drawing one: four ideas become four numbered objects. Key move — numbering the relics 1) 2) 3) 4) inside one sentence is what stops the model from blending them into a single glowing pile.
steps.prompt:
A wide 16-bit pixel-art RPG scene in the style of classic Castlevania games. A stone candle-lit shrine room inside a castle, with four ornate stone pedestals in a row, each holding a glowing relic on a velvet cushion: 1) an ancient open grimoire glowing pale blue, 2) a silver shield with a small pulsing rune gauge, 3) a leather satchel with glowing tagged vials, 4) an enchanted magnifying lens over a gear-shaped talisman.
Style: classic Castlevania pixel art, chunky readable pixels, gothic stonework, dithered shading, engraved stone arches behind each pedestal.
Lighting: warm flickering torchlight and candle glow on each relic, deep purple shadows, cobwebs in the corners, faint dust motes in torch beams.
Composition: wide banner, four pedestals evenly spaced, symmetrical, centered, cathedral-like stone room framing.
Constraints: no readable paragraph text, no logos, no watermark, no brand marks.

steps.title: 3. Stat altar — core limits
steps.text: Abstract settings turned into three physical gauges you can actually see. Key move — every setting becomes a physical object: liquid meter, falling hourglass, stacked orbs. Models render objects, not abstractions.
steps.prompt:
A wide 16-bit pixel-art RPG scene in the style of classic Castlevania games. A gothic stone altar room with three enchanted stained-glass windows set into the wall, each glowing with a different magical gauge: the left window shows a rising liquid blood-red meter (a scroll-length measure), the center window shows a glowing hourglass with sand mid-fall, the right window shows three stacked crystal orbs of increasing size (small, medium, large) each faintly lit.
Style: classic Castlevania pixel art, chunky readable pixels, ornate gothic stone carvings framing each window, dithered shading.
Lighting: cold moonlight through the glass mixing with warm candle sconces below each window, deep purple-black shadows, subtle magical particle glow.
Composition: wide banner, three windows evenly spaced, symmetrical, centered, cathedral wall framing.
Constraints: no readable paragraph text, no logos, no watermark, no brand marks.

steps.title: 4. Equip altar — prompt anatomy
steps.text: Five prompt parts drawn as five orbiting relics — metaphor and lesson in one object. Key move — inline parentheses — mask (identity), gauntlet (action), spyglass (camera) — lock a 1:1 mapping the model cannot shuffle.
steps.prompt:
A wide 16-bit pixel-art RPG scene in the style of classic Castlevania games. A vampire hunter stands on a stone ritual circle in a candle-lit armory, arms slightly raised, surrounded by five glowing floating relics orbiting him at chest height: a carved wooden mask (identity), a gauntlet wrapped in chain (action), a brass spyglass (camera/viewpoint), a stained-glass shard glowing with shifting color (style), and a small lantern casting colored light (light & color).
Style: classic Castlevania pixel art, chunky readable pixels, gothic armory stonework, dithered shading, engraved ritual circle on the floor.
Lighting: candle glow mixed with each relic's own colored magic light, deep purple shadows, faint incense smoke curling upward.
Composition: wide banner, hunter centered, five relics evenly arranged in an arc around him.
Constraints: no readable paragraph text, no logos, no watermark, no brand marks.

steps.title: 5. Corridor fork — do's & don'ts
steps.text: One frame that argues with itself — safe path left, cursed path right, zero text. Key move — declaring "split composition" in the first sentence makes the model render two mini-scenes instead of one blurred average.
steps.prompt:
A wide 16-bit pixel-art RPG scene in the style of classic Castlevania games, split composition inside a castle corridor fork. Left half: a sturdy stone-tiled corridor lit by warm steady torches, intact banners on the wall, a confident vampire hunter silhouette walking forward. Right half: a crumbling corridor with cracked broken tiles, a chasm gap, swinging spiked pendulum traps, and sickly green-red witch-light glow.
Style: classic Castlevania pixel art, chunky readable pixels, gothic stone architecture, dithered shading, cobwebs on the cursed side.
Lighting: warm amber torchlight on the left, sickly toxic-green and blood-red glow on the right, both set against shared deep purple-black stone.
Composition: wide banner, clear left/right split down the center, symmetrical framing, single stone archway dividing the two paths.
Constraints: no readable paragraph text, no logos, no watermark, no brand marks.

steps.title: 6. Castle map — the workflow
steps.text: A map screen doing double duty as a four-stage process diagram. Key move — "ascending left-to-right" converts a floor plan into a timeline: the eye walks the workflow in the right order.
steps.prompt:
A wide 16-bit pixel-art RPG scene in the style of a classic Castlevania castle map / overworld screen. Four gothic chambers connected by a winding stone stairway path rising left to right across a cross-section of a haunted castle: 1) a small candle-lit study with a sketch on a lectern (draft), 2) a mid tower room with a spinning hourglass and looping chain motif (iterate), 3) a workshop chamber with an anvil and glowing tools (refine), 4) the highest throne chamber with a lit brazier and banner (finalize).
Style: classic Castlevania pixel-art map screen, chunky readable pixels, cross-section castle silhouette, dithered shading, gothic stonework.
Lighting: warm golden torchlight tracing the stairway path between chambers, deep indigo night sky with bats and a crescent moon behind the towers.
Composition: wide banner, ascending left-to-right path, four chambers evenly spaced along the castle's height.
Constraints: no readable paragraph text, no logos, no watermark, no brand marks.

steps.title: 7. Boss fight — troubleshooting
steps.text: The error state as a character, with the corruption scoped to one body. Key move — scoping the damage — "molten fissures are the only corrupted element" — keeps the hero and the hall clean pixel art. Even an error-state concept stays purely visual: no "ERROR" text anywhere in the frame.
steps.prompt:
A wide 16-bit pixel-art RPG boss-battle scene in the style of classic Castlevania games. A vampire hunter braces with his whip in a grand castle hall, facing a large stone gargoyle boss with glowing molten-orange cracks running across its stone body, its eyes glowing an unstable flickering red.
Style: classic Castlevania pixel art, chunky readable pixels, gothic hall architecture, dithered shading. The gargoyle's cracked-stone texture and molten fissures are the only "corrupted" element — clean pixel art everywhere else, no static, no scanlines, no color noise, no scattered particle grain anywhere in the image, wings and background stay crisp and fully rendered.
Lighting: warning-style flickering red and amber glow radiating from the gargoyle's cracks, deep indigo hall shadows, hunter rim-lit by torchlight.
Composition: wide banner, hunter on the left, corrupted gargoyle boss on the right, dynamic confrontation pose, tension in the stance.
Constraints: no readable paragraph text, no logos, no watermark, no brand marks, no glitch/static/noise overlay, no scattered colored pixel grain.

steps.title: 8. Throne room — victory lap
steps.text: Ask for a banner shape and the model will fill it with invented letters unless you stop it in the same sentence. Key move — "an ornate empty stone banner/plaque shape low in frame (no text inside it)" names the shape and forbids its contents in one breath. It holds: there is no readable lettering anywhere in the eight images, plaque included.
steps.prompt:
A wide 16-bit pixel-art RPG victory scene in the style of classic Castlevania games. A vampire hunter stands triumphant on the steps of a grand throne room, holding a glowing ornate relic/artifact high above his head, coiled whip at his belt, one boot resting on a fallen bat-winged gargoyle statue fragment. Tall stained-glass windows behind him flood the hall with moonlight; a soft shower of pixel dust and golden light motes drifts down from above.
Style: classic Castlevania pixel art, chunky readable pixels, gothic throne room architecture, dithered shading, dramatic hero silhouette pose.
Lighting: warm golden light rays bursting from the raised relic, cool blue moonlight through stained glass, deep purple-black shadows in the corners.
Composition: wide banner, hunter centered on a raised stone dais, an ornate empty stone banner/plaque shape low in frame (no text inside it).
Constraints: no readable paragraph text anywhere, no logos, no watermark, no brand marks.

steps.title: 9. What the style block does not lock
steps.text: The world held across all eight images and the hunter did not. He leaves image 01 in a tattered dark-blue coat with short hair; by image 04 the coat is black with crimson lining, a long red cape has appeared that no prompt asked for, and the hair is past his shoulders. Look at the prompts above and the cause is obvious: the Style, Lighting, Composition and Constraints block was pasted into all eight word-for-word — the sentence describing the man was rewritten every time. A style block locks the architecture, the palette and the pixel size. It does not lock the cast. If the same character has to appear in every frame, treat his description as part of the style block and copy it verbatim, or feed image 01 back in as a reference and generate the rest from it.
steps.result_label: Two images from the final pack · 01 castle gate and 04 equip altar
steps.result_caption: Same series, same style block, same hunter on paper. Dark-blue coat and short hair on the left; black-and-crimson coat, full red cape and long hair on the right.

guides.result: An eight-image RPG asset pack in a locked Castlevania style, plus the prompt anatomy behind it: how to render a list, a setting, a metaphor, a do/don't, a workflow and an error state without ever asking the model to write text — and one honest failure, a hero who changes clothes between frames because the style block never described him.

guides.title: Winter ops: a 41-second FPS route that holds the world and loses the gun
guides.desc: One first-person route through five spaces: a dusty bunker room, a pipe tunnel, a steel door into a wet container yard with a yellow forklift, a frosted ledge above the yard, and a hall with snow on the floor and a tracked vehicle. The world holds. The rifle does not — and that turns out to be the useful part.

steps.title: Write the route as doors, not as shots
steps.text: Continuation holds when every space has a physical exit into the next one. Do not list five scenes — list one walk. The strongest link in this render is a steel door: the tunnel ends at it, the yard starts behind it, and the light change does the work an edit would normally do.
steps.prompt: First-person shooter cinematic, photoreal, overcast winter. One continuous walk: (1) dusty bunker room, light shaft through a broken window. (2) Down into a utility tunnel — pipe runs overhead, fluorescent strips, standing water. (3) Reach a steel door with a fire extinguisher beside it, push through into grey daylight. (4) A container yard: stacked shipping containers, a yellow forklift, wet asphalt, fog on the treeline.
steps.result_caption: Tunnel, steel door, container yard in four seconds with no cut. The door swings outward and the camera never stops — the grey wall box beside the extinguisher is still on the left as the yard comes in.

steps.title: Expect the weapon to drift, and plan the cut list around it
steps.text: The world survived the extension. The rifle did not: it leaves the bunker as a black carbine with a red-dot sight and arrives in the last room as an olive rifle with a different body and optic. No prompt wording fixed this. What works is editorial — keep the weapon out of frame across the joins, or cut on a reload, which is exactly what happens at 0:13 here.
steps.result_label: Two frames from the final render · 0:06 and 0:36
steps.result_caption: Same route, thirty seconds apart. Black polymer carbine with a red-dot on the left; olive rifle, different receiver and optic, on the right.

steps.title: Extend from the last frame, upscale once
steps.text: Each segment starts from the previous segment's final frame — the source file for this piece is named segment_01_continuation. The stitched master is 2560×1440, 184 MB; the page serves a 1080p H.264 cut instead. One note on the yard while you watch: it is wet asphalt and fog, not snow. Snow only turns up later, on the ledge above the containers and on the floor of the final hall.

guides.result: A 41-second first-person walk that keeps its geometry, its route and its grey winter light across five spaces — and loses the rifle twice along the way. Both halves of that are in the clip.

guides.title: Anime caramel pudding: a recipe told in ten shots
guides.desc: Sugar melting in a pan, caramel into the tin, eggs whisked, custard through a sieve, the tin on the oven rack, the unmoulding, the spoon going in — ten shots in fifteen seconds, and only in the last two does a lavender-haired girl in red headphones get to taste it.

steps.title: Write the recipe as the shot list
steps.text: Food anime works because the process is the plot. Do not describe "a cooking scene" — list the actual steps of a caramel pudding in order and give each one a close-up. The model cannot invent a recipe, but it can illustrate one.
steps.prompt: Anime cooking sequence, clean cel-shaded 2D style, soft kitchen light, warm palette. Close-ups in recipe order: (1) white sugar melting in a dark pan over a blue gas flame, one amber patch spreading. (2) the finished caramel poured into a round metal tin. (3) egg yolks and sugar whisked in a glass bowl. (4) custard strained through a fine mesh sieve into a second glass bowl. (5) custard poured into the tin on top of the set caramel. (6) the tin on an oven rack, element glowing orange. (7) hands lifting the tin away to unmould, caramel flooding down the sides onto a white plate. (8) a spoon pressing into the wobble, caramel pooling.
steps.result_caption: Three shots in four seconds — sugar melting, caramel into the tin, yolks whisked. Cuts land at 0:01.4 and 0:02.4, exactly where the recipe moves on.

steps.title: Reveal the character last
steps.text: Six shots of hands and food, then let her in gradually: at 0:09 you get a torso in a white shirt lifting the tin, and only at 0:13 a face. Describe her once, precisely, and reuse that sentence verbatim — otherwise the last shot arrives as a generic anime girl and the whole sequence reads as stock.
steps.prompt: Final shot: a young woman with long lavender hair and red over-ear headphones, white shirt, eyes closed in delight, tasting a spoonful of caramel pudding in a bright kitchen with a window and hanging utensils. Same cel-shaded style, same kitchen.
steps.result_caption: Her face gets 1.8 seconds of a 15-second clip. Lavender hair, red over-ear headphones, white shirt — same kitchen, same window, same hanging utensils as the shots before it.

steps.title: Upscale the master, deliver 1080p
steps.text: The master is 3840×2160 HEVC, 91 MB. Flat cel shading is mostly large areas of one colour, so it compresses far harder than live action: the 1080p H.264 version on this page is 4.6 MB at 24 fps — about one twentieth the size. Grain-heavy footage never does that. Play the clip above.

guides.result: A 15-second cel-shaded clip that follows a real caramel-pudding method in the right order — caramel first, custard strained before it goes in, unmould after baking — in one kitchen, ending on a face you only meet at 0:13.

guides.title: Faux-real: four scans, one 10-second loop, not a single cut
guides.desc: Four Gaussian-splat scans in a raw viewport — a girl at a green payphone, a kitchen with a dirt bike parked in it, a supermarket aisle, a girl kneeling at an open fridge. They are joined by collapsing each scan into a ball of points and rebuilding the next one out of it, so a scene-detector finds zero cuts in the whole clip.

steps.title: Leave the capture UI switched on
steps.text: Every scan here floats on flat grey as an island with a crumbling edge — shoot tight, one person and one object cluster, and stop walking before the room ends. Then resist cleaning up the viewport. The dashed bounding box, the white corner handles, the green pose skeleton, the dotted face-landmark mask and three or four stray mouse cursors are what sell this as captured data rather than a render. Remove them and it is just a grainy photo.
steps.result_caption: One slab of pavement, a green payphone, a bollard, a girl on the handset — and over it the bounding box, the skeleton, the face dots and four cursors nobody bothered to move.

steps.title: Change scene by collapsing the cloud, never by cutting
steps.text: Each scan holds still for a slow orbit, then blows apart: the points rush the camera, gather into a rough sphere, and unfold into the next location. Nothing else in the clip moves fast. Run a scene-detector over the final file and it reports zero cuts across ten seconds — the transitions are inside the geometry, so there is no frame where two images sit next to each other.
steps.result_caption: Payphone collapses to a ball of points at 0:02, the kitchen builds itself out of the same points by 0:02.5, orbits for a second, then blows apart again into the supermarket aisle.

steps.title: Land back on the first scan
steps.text: Close the loop on the scene you opened with: the payphone island at 0:09.9 sits at almost the same camera angle as 0:00, so the restart is invisible. Note the supermarket breaks the pattern deliberately — the camera is inside that scan rather than orbiting an island, which is what stops four floating dioramas from feeling like a template. Master 1440×1440, delivered 1080×1080 H.264, 5.4 MB, 24 fps.

guides.result: A 1080×1080 loop, 10.1 seconds, four scans, zero cuts — the point noise at every boundary is the transition mechanism rather than an artefact to clean up.

guides.title: Graphics Lab: 37 shader scenes that report their own physics
guides.desc: A screen walk through a Render Library running on 127.0.0.1:4180 — snow accumulation, wet-puddle rain, a raytraced diamond, spectral glass, a procedural F1 car, planet surfaces, aurora. The header counts 37 scenes; the status bar under each one prints the grating pitch and diffraction orders it is actually solving.

steps.title: Give the agent a taxonomy, not a wish list
steps.text: The library has categories because the brief had categories. Ask for named groups and the app builds a rail with a count against each one — Precipitation Surfaces 2, Procedural Architecture 1, Procedural Geometry 5, Procedural Materials 5, Procedural Planets 1, Procedural Vegetation 5, and more below the fold. Those counts are the point: 37 scenes in a flat list is a dump, 37 scenes with a 1 next to Architecture tells you exactly which skill is untested.
steps.prompt: Build a local Render Library web app (Three.js). Left rail: scene groups — Precipitation Surfaces, Procedural Architecture, Procedural Geometry, Procedural Materials, Procedural Planets, Procedural Vegetation. Main grid: one live WebGL card per scene with title and OPEN. Header: search "find a system, effect or technique", Rescan, Overview. Dark UI, Quadcode palette.
steps.result_caption: 37 SCENES and ENGINE READY in the rail header; the search box still carries the placeholder from the brief, "find a system, effect or technique…". Every card is a live WebGL view with an OPEN link, not a thumbnail.

steps.title: Make each scene print the physics it is solving
steps.text: A demo that only looks right is untestable. Ask for a status bar that exposes the actual model parameters, not just frame rate. Open the diffraction grating and the bar reads FPS 17 · DRAWS 566 · TRIANGLES 21 · PITCHNM · STRIPSAMPLES 21 · ORDERS 1–3 at 1280 × 720 — grating pitch in nanometres and the diffraction orders being summed. That line is the difference between a rainbow texture and a rainbow that is being computed, and it is what turns the library into a regression suite you can read at a glance.
steps.prompt: Every scene opens in a viewer with: a resolution selector (1280×720 up to full frame), Pause, Reload, Capture, Full Frame. Fixed status bar along the bottom: READY state, FPS, DRAWS, TRIANGLES, then the scene's own physical parameters — for Physical Diffraction Grating expose grating pitch in nm, strip samples and diffraction orders. Print the render resolution at the right end.
steps.result_caption: A holographic card tilting under a diffraction shader. Watch the bottom bar, not the card: FPS, draw calls, grating pitch and orders 1–3 update as it turns.

steps.title: Record the walkthrough at 30 fps
steps.text: Screen capture defaults to 60 fps, which is wasted on a clip that is mostly a static UI with one moving viewport. This walkthrough is 41 seconds at 1792×1080, 30 fps, 10.4 MB — half the bitrate, no visible cost, and it stays under the 12 MB budget. Note the honest number on screen while you watch: the diffraction scene runs at 17 fps. Play the clip above.

guides.result: A browsable render library — 37 live WebGL scenes across precipitation, procedural geometry, PBR materials, planets and vegetation — where every scene reports its own frame rate, draw calls and physical parameters, so a broken skill shows up as a number rather than as a vibe.

guides.title: Custom controller store: hide the skin swap inside a rotation
guides.desc: A PS5-controller landing page where the hero is a real 3D model — 007 First Light gold, Genshin Impact white-and-blue, God of War crimson. Arrows at the bottom change skin; the page turns the controller edge-on for a third of a second to do it, and re-themes the headline, copy, price panel, side cards and background tint in the same beat.

steps.title: Re-theme the whole page, not just the model
steps.text: A configurator that only recolours the product looks like a demo. Specify the skin as a theme: headline, body copy, the colour of the Add to cart pill, the background tint, the trailer card in the corner and the two stacked cards of the other skins all change together. Keep the furniture identical — same nav, same $79.99, same battery and latency cards — so the eye reads one page in two states rather than two pages.
steps.prompt: Build a product landing page for custom PS5 controllers. Hero: full-viewport 3D controller (Three.js, GLB), slow auto-rotate, drag to orbit, soft studio lighting, floor reflection. Skins as material sets: "007 First Light" — brushed gold with black grips; "Genshin Impact" — pearl white with cyan glow accents; "God of War" — matte crimson with white face plate. Left column: eyebrow, skin name as a two-line headline, three lines of copy, Add to cart pill and $79.99. Right: the two other skins as stacked cards, nearest one larger. Bottom left: a trailer card with the skin name and a play button. Bottom right: two stat cards, 12 hr · Battery Life and 1 ms · Low Latency. Each skin is a theme — headline, copy, pill colour and background tint all change with it.
steps.result_label: Two frames from the final render · 0:03 and 0:08
steps.result_caption: Same layout, two skins. Headline, body copy, trailer card, background tint and the two side cards all swap; the nav, the $79.99 and the battery and latency cards stay put.

steps.title: Turn the model edge-on to cover the swap
steps.text: Crossfading one controller into another shows you the crossfade. This page does something better: on the arrow press the UI fades out, the hero spins to edge-on — where it is a few pixels of silhouette and there is nothing left to see — and the new skin unfolds out of that rotation. The whole exchange takes about 0.6 s and there is no frame in which two controllers overlap.
steps.prompt: On next/previous: fade the text column, trailer card and stat cards to zero over ~200 ms while rotating the hero 90° to a side-on view. At the narrowest point switch the material set and the side cards, then rotate back and fade the new theme in. Total ~600 ms, eased, never linear.
steps.result_caption: Cursor hits the right arrow, the page empties, the controller narrows to a sliver at 0:05.7 — and comes back crimson as God of War.

steps.title: Prove the model is real by showing its back
steps.text: Anyone can fake a product hero with three renders. One drag that carries the controller all the way round settles it — and it only works if the back is textured too. Here the orbit runs from 0:08 to 0:13 and passes through the rear shell, where the God of War omega sits between the grips. Record the browser at 60 fps for a smooth orbit and conform to 30 for delivery: this clip is 13.6 s at 1820×1080, 2.8 MB.
steps.result_caption: Mid-orbit, looking at the back of the controller: the omega mark, the grip seams and the rear shell are all modelled.

steps.title: Watch the full clip
steps.text: Genshin state, arrow press, swap, then a full turn around the God of War shell. Play the clip above.

guides.result: A product-configurator hero where the skin change is hidden inside a 90° rotation and the whole page re-themes with it — and where one drag to the back of the shell proves there is a real model underneath, not three renders.

guides.title: Seoul arcade on MiniDV: 14 seconds in one take, and no cut to black
guides.desc: A young woman pushes into a small neighbourhood arcade, drifts past the cabinets, sits down at a fighting machine and the tape runs out on a glowing screen. Written as an early-2000s Sony MiniDV home video with the faults kept in — and the faults are measurable: the auto-iris overshoots by 68% at the door, and a scene detector finds no hard cut anywhere in the first 14.3 seconds.

steps.title: Describe the camera as the main character
steps.text: What sells MiniDV is not the location — it is the mistakes, and you have to name them one by one: late follow, auto-iris overshoot at the door, focus hunting between bright screens and faces, DV compression, mic distortion. It shows up in the signal, not just in the vibe: average luma runs 83 at the first frame, overshoots to 139 by 0:00.9 as the street light hits the sensor, and takes another 1.7 seconds to settle back to 94. Nobody graded that in — the prompt asked for exposure pumping and the render produced a real one. Write "cinematic" anywhere and you lose all of it.
steps.prompt: Main Subject: Young Korean woman, 24, naturally attractive, realistic skin, minimal makeup, long blonde hair loosely tied back. Loose cream cardigan over a faded red T-shirt, relaxed blue jeans, white sneakers, thin silver necklace. Preserve her exact identity throughout. Location: small old-fashioned Seoul neighborhood arcade, early evening — dim fluorescent light, rows of aging cabinets, colorful screens, scratched floor, plastic stools, faded posters, coin machines, tangled cables, a few local teenagers in the background, warm street light through the entrance. Style: ultra-realistic early-2000s Sony MiniDV home video. Heavy handheld shake, awkward framing, autofocus hunting between bright screens and faces, exposure pumping, faded colors, soft contrast, DV compression, slight motion blur and microphone distortion. No stabilization, no modern cinematic movement.
steps.result_caption: Four seconds at the door. The frame blows out as she steps in and claws its way back — luma 83 → 139 → 94, all of it generated, none of it added afterwards.

steps.title: Write one beat where the camera stops moving
steps.text: Five timestamped beats, fifteen seconds — and the useful thing is what the model did with them. It did not cut five times; it delivered one unbroken take, and it varied the shake instead. Run a scene detector at a low threshold and it fires roughly every second frame while she is walking, then goes completely silent from 0:07.0 to 0:09.9 — the three seconds she is sat at the cabinet. That pause is the whole clip. Handheld footage that shakes uniformly for fifteen seconds reads as a filter; handheld footage that settles when the operator sits down reads as a person.
steps.prompt: 00:00–00:03: she pushes the arcade door and steps inside; the camera follows late, briefly overexposing from the bright street before adjusting. 00:03–00:06: she walks past machines deciding what to play; the camera wanders to other screens before finding her. 00:06–00:09: she sits at an old fighting-game cabinet and plays, competitive, leaning in, rapid button presses, camera shaking behind her. 00:09–00:12: she wins a round, small fist pump, proud grin to camera — then loses the next round instantly and bursts out laughing. 00:12–00:15: she stands and walks to another machine; the camera accidentally zooms tight onto a glowing screen, autofocus struggles against the pixels, and the recording cuts to black. Audio: arcade ambience only — buttons, joysticks, game sounds, coin mechanisms, fluorescent buzz, distant talk, footsteps, laughter. No music, no narration.
steps.result_caption: The quiet three seconds. She is at the cabinet, the operator has stopped walking, and this is the only stretch of the tape where the scene detector registers nothing at all.

steps.title: Check the ending you asked for — this one did not arrive
steps.text: The prompt ends with "the recording cuts to black". It does not. Run a black-frame detector over the delivered file and it finds zero black segments: the last half-second flares instead, luma spiking to 173 as the lens swings onto a glowing cabinet, then dropping to 17 on the final two frames — dark, but never black. It happens to work, because a tape running out on a bright screen is more convincing than a clean fade. The lesson is the check, not the luck: verify the last beat of every render before you publish a claim about it. Then watermark bottom-centre at 10% width, upscale 2× once, and leave the grain alone — the DV artifacts are the style. Play the clip above.
steps.result_label: Frames from the final render · 0:14.85 and 0:15.00
steps.result_caption: The two frames the prompt called a cut to black: a blown-out flare at luma 173, then a dark-but-not-black final frame at 17. A black-frame detector finds nothing in the whole file.

guides.result: 15.07 seconds of believable found footage in a single take — measured exposure pumping at the door, three seconds of stillness at the cabinet, and an ending that ignored the instruction and came out better for it.

guides.title: Rooftop run: a cel-shaded action trailer in 30 seconds
guides.desc: A green-tunic hero sprints, vaults and leaps across the tiled roofs of a storybook town and up a castle wall — one continuous chase, cel-shaded, cut to 30 seconds.

steps.title: Lock the hero and the palette before any motion
steps.text: Trailers fall apart when the hero changes between shots. Describe the character once — silhouette, colors, weapon — and the world once — terracotta roofs, teal shutters, midday sky. Every shot prompt reuses that block verbatim.
steps.prompt: Cel-shaded action-adventure game cinematic. Hero: young swordsman in a green tunic and pointed cap, brown boots, small shield on the back, blond hair. World: medieval storybook town — terracotta tiled roofs, cream stucco walls, teal shutters, cobblestone plaza with market stalls, bright midday sun, cumulus clouds. Clean toon outlines, saturated colors, stylized grass and foliage.
steps.result_caption: Hero, palette and ink outline fixed in frame one. Every later shot inherits exactly this.

steps.title: Direct the chase as a rooftop-to-castle route
steps.text: Give the model a route, not a mood. Roof ridge → gap jump → plaza overlook → drop into the square → castle wall climb. Each beat is 4–6 seconds; the camera stays behind and slightly above so parkour reads clearly.
steps.prompt: Shot list, same hero and world block: (1) hero sprints along a roof ridge, camera chasing from behind. (2) Long jump across an alley gap, tiles crumble. (3) Slides down a roof into the market plaza, vendors look up. (4) Runs along the top of the castle curtain wall, blue banners with a gold crest. (5) Leaps toward a tower window, freeze on the jump. Continuous motion, no cuts inside a shot.
steps.result_caption: Market rooftops into the castle wall. The chase is a route with a destination, not a loop.

steps.title: Cut on the jumps, upscale to 4K, deliver at 1080p
steps.text: Cut each transition at the apex of a jump — motion hides the seam. Upscale the master to 4K for the archive, then encode a 1080p H.264 delivery under 12 MB for the web. Play the clip above.

guides.result: A 30-second cel-shaded chase trailer with one hero, one town and one castle — consistent character, consistent light, no cut feels like a model switch.

guides.title: Blocky world, photoreal remaster
guides.desc: Four iconic voxel biomes — vine-choked temple, red desert, glowing portal pool, oak-and-brick house — re-rendered as photoreal environments while the blocky character stays blocky.

steps.title: Pick four biomes people recognize instantly
steps.text: The joke lands only if the source is obvious. Jungle temple, desert with dead bushes, an obsidian portal by water, a starter house with a boxy character. Each gets one slow camera move, nothing else.
steps.prompt: Photoreal remaster of a voxel sandbox world. Keep every shape cubic — blocks, stairs, one-meter grid — but render with physically based materials: mossy sandstone, wind-blown sand, obsidian with purple portal glow, oak planks and cobblestone. Cinematic lighting, shallow depth of field, ray-traced reflections, 4K detail.
steps.result_caption: Desert into water. Two of the four biomes, recognisable before the transition finishes.

steps.title: Keep the geometry blocky, push everything else
steps.text: Tell the model explicitly what may not change: block grid, proportions, the character's cube head. Everything else — textures, light, atmosphere, foliage density — goes to maximum realism.
steps.prompt: Shot 1: slow push through a ruined jungle temple corridor, vines and light shafts. Shot 2: pan across a red desert with dry bushes and a distant plateau. Shot 3: obsidian portal frame beside a lily-pad pond, purple glow reflecting. Shot 4: a boxy character stands in front of a brick-and-oak house with a hedge; the character is low-poly cubic, the world around it photoreal.
steps.result_caption: Cubic lily pads, photoreal water. Geometry stays blocky; light, texture and volume do not.

steps.title: Upscale and grade as one reel
steps.text: Run one color grade across all four so they read as one world. Upscale to 4K, deliver 1080p. Play the clip above.

guides.result: A 30-second remaster reel: photoreal light, materials and foliage on a world whose geometry is still cubes — the contrast is the whole idea.

guides.title: Metro ruins: first-person walkthrough with live fire
guides.desc: A first-person sweep through a bombed-out school and flooded corridor — weapon in frame, muzzle flash, dust in the light — the vertical-slice shot a shooter pitch needs.

steps.title: Describe the weapon as a fixed object in the frame
steps.text: First-person clips break when the gun morphs. Describe it as a prop bolted to the camera: position, finish, attachments. Repeat that block in every shot.
steps.prompt: First-person shooter cinematic, photoreal. Weapon fixed lower-right in frame: modern assault rifle, matte black, holographic sight, tan foregrip, worn edges. Environment: abandoned Soviet-era school — peeling green paint, shattered windows, overturned desks, chalkboard, dust hanging in light shafts. Overcast daylight, muted palette, slight lens dirt.
steps.result_caption: Mid-burst and the rifle has not changed shape since the first frame. "Prop bolted to the camera" did that.

steps.title: Route the walkthrough room by room
steps.text: Corridor → classroom → stairwell → open yard. One direction of travel, one turn per shot. Put the single firefight in the widest room so the muzzle flash has something to light.
steps.prompt: Shot 1: advance down a flooded concrete corridor, flashlight beam. Shot 2: enter a classroom, sweep left across desks and blackboard. Shot 3: contact — three quick shots toward a doorway, muzzle flash lights the dust, casings eject. Shot 4: climb a collapsed stairwell into daylight. Shot 5: overlook a ruined courtyard with a distant apartment block.
steps.result_caption: Classroom into stairwell. One direction of travel, one turn — the room-by-room route from step 2.

steps.title: Cut tight, add a low-end mix, deliver
steps.text: Keep 4–5 seconds per shot and let the gunfire cut carry the edit. Deliver 1080p H.264. Play the clip above.

guides.result: A 25-second first-person concept sequence with a consistent weapon model, readable level geometry and one clear moment of contact.

guides.title: Interior render battle: Fable 5.1 vs GPT-6 Astra
guides.desc: One architecture brief, two video models, split-screen with labels — exterior approach, entry, living room, kitchen. Same beats, two different interior designers.

steps.title: Write one walkthrough brief both models receive
steps.text: The comparison is only honest if the prompt is identical. Fix the route and the camera; leave material and style choices to each model so their taste shows.
steps.prompt: Architectural walkthrough, photoreal. Route: (1) slow approach to a single-storey Mediterranean villa, terracotta roof, white stucco, arched entry. (2) Push through the arched front door. (3) Reveal an open-plan living room with a low sofa, large black-framed windows, wood floor. (4) End on the kitchen island with pendant lights. Smooth gimbal motion, golden-hour light, 4K.
steps.result_caption: Same living room, same brief, two models side by side. Differences you see are the models', not the prompt's.

steps.title: Generate on both, do not cherry-pick
steps.text: Take the first clean run from each model. Re-rolling one side until it wins is the fastest way to make the format worthless.
steps.result_caption: The kitchen pass on both. Neither take was regenerated — this is the first output each model returned.

steps.title: Cut the split-screen with labels and one music bed
steps.text: Both takes in sync, model names bottom-left and bottom-right, one track across the whole thing. Play the clip above.

guides.result: A 26-second labeled split-screen where two models walk the same house — the format that gets "left or right?" in the comments.

guides.title: Arcade fighter: one pixel-art round, full HUD
guides.desc: A 15-second 2D fighting-game round — two fighters, sunset temple stage, health bars, timer, hit sparks — generated as if captured from a 90s arcade cabinet.

steps.title: Specify the HUD as part of the image
steps.text: Models drop UI unless it is described as pixels on screen. Health bars, round timer, player tags — name them, place them, color them.
steps.prompt: 16-bit arcade fighting game, side view, pixel art. HUD: two green-to-red health bars top-left and top-right, yellow round timer "99" centered, "P1"/"P2" tags. Stage: Japanese temple courtyard at sunset, orange sky, purple clouds, paper lanterns. Fighters: left — orange gi, black hair, bare feet; right — purple vest, headband, dark trousers. Chunky pixels, limited palette, CRT-clean.
steps.result_caption: Health bars, timer, round counter — all rendered as part of the image, not overlaid.

steps.title: Choreograph six hits, not a brawl
steps.text: Give the round a shape: poke, block, launcher, air juggle, fireball, KO. One exchange per shot, sprites always at the same scale.
steps.prompt: Sequence: (1) fighters face off, idle bounce. (2) Right fighter dashes in, left blocks — white spark. (3) Left uppercut launches right into the air. (4) Right recovers, jumping kick. (5) Left throws a blue fireball across the stage, big hit flash. (6) Right collapses, "KO" moment. Sprite scale constant, background static except lanterns swaying.
steps.result_caption: The first two of six choreographed hits. Each has a wind-up and a landing you can count.

steps.title: Add the watermark and deliver at native 1080p
steps.text: Pixel art has no business being upscaled. Encode straight to 1080p H.264. Play the clip above.

guides.result: A complete fighting-game round in pixel art with HUD, hit effects and a KO — the reference clip a retro-fighter pitch deck is missing.

guides.title: Forest ops: rain, river, bunker — a tactical FPS teaser
guides.desc: First-person tactical sequence through a wet pine forest: rifle low, rain on the lens, river crossing, then into a dark bunker and a light at the end — with a CTA card.

steps.title: Set the weather as the main character
steps.text: Rain is what makes this feel expensive. Specify it everywhere: drops on the lens, wet bark, mist between trunks, water sheeting off the rifle.
steps.prompt: First-person tactical shooter, photoreal, heavy rain. Weapon fixed lower-center: modern carbine, olive-drab, red-dot sight, suppressor, rain beading on metal. Environment: dense pine forest, mossy boulders, ferns, low mist, overcast grey light, rain streaks on the lens.

steps.title: Move from open forest into a confined space
steps.text: Contrast sells the cut. Wide forest → river rocks → bunker doorway → black interior with a single light. The end card goes on the black.
steps.prompt: Shot 1: advance through pines, rifle low-ready. Shot 2: aim down sight across a rocky river, water rushing. Shot 3: cross the river on boulders, camera bobbing. Shot 4: approach a concrete bunker entrance in the hillside. Shot 5: enter the dark corridor, a single square of light at the far end. Hold on the light.

steps.title: Conform 60 fps to 30, upscale, end on the CTA
steps.text: The source ran at 60 fps; at web bitrates 30 fps keeps more detail per frame. Upscale to 4K for the master, deliver 1080p. Play the clip above.

guides.title: Crimson: jungle, shark, fortress — a third-person adventure trailer
guides.desc: A dark-haired adventurer crosses a jungle river, dives past a shark, scales a cliff and fights through a stone fortress — a 30-second third-person trailer with one consistent heroine.

steps.text: One paragraph, reused verbatim in every shot: hair, outfit, gear, build. This is the only way a third-person character survives five environments.

guides.title: Brazil street: a 10-second documentary walk
guides.desc: Golden-hour handheld follow of a woman walking a narrow Brazilian street — parked cars, tangled wires, haze — the kind of b-roll a doc opener is built on.

steps.title: Ask for documentary, not cinema
steps.text: The words matter: handheld, follow shot, natural light, no color push. Anything "cinematic" and the model adds crane moves and teal-orange.
steps.prompt: Documentary handheld follow shot, 35mm look, natural golden-hour backlight with haze. Subject: young woman with long dark hair, white shirt, walking away from camera down a narrow street in a Brazilian city. Parked cars, low buildings, overhead power lines, warm dust in the air. steps.title: Upscale and grade lightly

guides.title: Restyle a physics-driven testimonial widget
guides.desc: Take a third-party Three.js testimonial widget (rope-physics puller, canvas-textured cards) and rebuild its whole visual language — CSS tokens, stage lighting, card typography and copy — to match the Quadcode dark UI, without touching the underlying rig.

steps.title: 1. Audit the source before touching anything
steps.text: The original repo ships a warm cream/terracotta editorial theme: Georgia serif headline, #C2603C terracotta accent, paper-grain canvas cards. None of it is Quadcode — but the rig underneath (rope physics, drag-to-scroll, canvas-painted cards) is solid and worth keeping untouched.
steps.prompt: Clone the target repo, run it locally, and list every hardcoded visual value: CSS custom properties, font-family declarations, and any hex colors baked into the JS (canvas fill styles, Three.js material colors, light colors). Do not touch logic yet — only inventory.
